name: Guyana
summary: A will is largely free, but a court can order provision for a spouse, children and other dependants from the estate under the Family and Dependants Provision Act. Succession follows the common-law domicile rules and no choice of foreign law is given. Guyana has common-law trusts but is not in the Hague Trusts Convention, and no private-foundation law was found.
family_claims: The Family and Dependants Provision Act (Act 22 of 1990, as amended by Act 10 of 2012) lets a court order maintenance or provision for qualifying family and dependants out of the net estate, including where a will omits them.
foreign_law_note: Common-law rule (not confirmed in a Guyanese statute here): movables pass under the law of the deceased's domicile and land under the law of its location. No right to choose the law of nationality was found.
trust_note: Common-law trusts are available (Guyana is a common-law country). Guyana is not a party to the Hague Trusts Convention. No private foundation law was found; charities are handled through other statutes. The family-provision Act has anti-avoidance rules that may reach assets moved out of the estate.
open_questions: Chapter number of the Family and Dependants Provision Act is cited as 12:22 by the Ministry of Legal Affairs file and as 12:24 elsewhere; confirm.
Who qualifies as an applicant, the time limit, and whether trust assets fall in the net estate were not read.
Whether Guyana has a trust statute (beyond the common law and the Trustees Act) and whether foundations exist was not verified.
Domicile and conflict rules for succession were not sourced in a Guyanese statute or case.
